title: SOLID design principles in backend architecture
description: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion in production backends.

questions.text: An OrderService class validates order inputs, calculates tax rates, charges Stripe credit cards, generates a PDF invoice, and sends an SMTP confirmation email. Which SOLID principle does this class most directly violate?
questions.explanation: The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) states that a class should have only one reason to change. Combining tax logic, payment gateway integration, PDF rendering, and email transport gives this class multiple disparate business actors and reasons to change.

questions.text: How do you refactor an application containing an 'if (paymentType == "CREDIT_CARD") ... else if (paymentType == "PAYPAL") ... else if (paymentType == "CRYPTO")' block to adhere to the Open/Closed Principle (OCP)?

options.text: Replace the if-else chain with a switch statement inside the same method
Define a PaymentStrategy interface and register distinct strategy implementations in a factory or dependency injection container
Store all payment credentials in a JSON configuration file
Make all payment classes static singletons

questions.explanation: The Open/Closed Principle states software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. Introducing a PaymentStrategy interface allows adding new payment methods (e.g. Apple Pay) by creating new classes without modifying existing, tested checkout code.

questions.text: A base class 'ReadOnlyRepository' has a method 'getById(id)'. A subclass 'CachedRepository' overrides it, but throws an UnsupportedOperationException whenever a cache miss occurs. Which SOLID principle is violated?
questions.explanation: The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) requires that subclasses can replace parent classes without altering the correctness of the program. Strengthening preconditions, throwing unexpected exceptions, or weakening postconditions violates LSP.

questions.text: What is the primary architectural benefit of the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions)?

options.text: It makes SQL database queries execute with fewer table locks
It decouples core domain business rules from volatile infrastructure details (like specific databases, third-party APIs, or web frameworks), making code unit-testable via mocks
It eliminates the need for unit tests entirely
It compresses class bytecode in memory

questions.explanation: DIP decouples core business logic from external libraries and I/O. For instance, UserService depends on an abstract UserRepository interface rather than a concrete PostgresUserRepository, allowing in-memory testing without a live database.

questions.text: The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) suggests that creating many small, client-specific role interfaces is preferable to a single bloated, general-purpose interface.
questions.explanation: True. ISP states that no client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use. Breaking giant interfaces into role-focused interfaces (e.g. Reader, Writer, Closer instead of an all-in-one FileHandler) prevents unnecessary coupling.
